Here's the thing: "will they publish their numbers" was never actually the hard question. Almost anyone confident in their own performance will offer to publish flattering numbers — that costs them nothing and buys a lot of goodwill. The question that actually separates good faith from a maneuver is *who controls the terms of that accountability*, and there are three specific things worth checking before you take the offer at face value:

**Is it forward-committed or backward-reported?** A team dodging scrutiny will happily tell you what they *already shipped* — that's just bragging with extra formatting. A team genuinely accepting accountability commits to a date *before* the work is done, then gets measured against it. If their offer is "we'll show you our hit rate," ask specifically: are you committing forecasts in advance, or reporting outcomes after the fact? Same words, very different animals.

**Who defines the metric and who audits it?** If they design their own dashboard, pick their own definition of "on time," and report it to you privately with no comparability to anyone else's numbers, that's not accountability — that's a controlled leak of information they already frame. Real accountability means the same metric definition, reviewed in the same forum as everyone else, where the numbers can actually be compared against other teams'.

**Does it come with the same standing as everyone else, or does it stay a private arrangement just between you and them?** This is the one that actually answers your two-tier worry too. If this becomes a quiet side deal nobody else sees, you've built exactly the two-tier system you were afraid of, just with better PR. If instead you fold their offer into the same public forecast review you'd eventually set up for everyone — same room, same cadence, same metric, they just happen to hit it without sprints — then it's not a dodge, it's the pilot case for the standard, arriving early and self-selected.

So don't answer their offer with yes or no. Answer it with the terms: "Great — publish it forward-looking, in the same review as every other team, using the metric I set, starting this cycle, permanently, not just until this blows over." If they say yes without flinching, your suspicion was wrong and you've gotten ahead of schedule on the thing you were going to build anyway. If they hedge on any of those three — want it private, want to self-define it, want it temporary — that hedge is the tell.
